Introduction Machine vision applications vary according to the technique used. Each image contains noise and deformation. Humans do not need to ﬁlter and remove noise to understand what is seen, but machine vision requires this to process an image. One task of vision is to detect and track humans under different environmental conditions. It is difﬁcult to track a human as the object under uncontrolled lighting conditions, in a crowded environment, or when the camera is in motion. These conditions can cause loss of information from the received image, such as the color, texture and shape of the object, which can be important to successful detection of the target. Most methods of target detection use image indices [1–4]. Pedestrian detection is usually done in two steps: feature extrac- tion and classiﬁcation. Feature extraction is preferred over the direct use of the raw pixels from images. One reason is that feature-based systems are quicker than raw pixel-based systems [5]. In the classiﬁcation stage, feature-based systems ﬁrst extract the features and the performance of the classiﬁer is highly depen- dent on the feature extracted. The proper selection of feature extraction and classiﬁcation methods improves the detection rate. Haar-like features are composed of a number of black and white areas for which the intensities of the pixels in the black and white areas are calculated separately. The feature value is obtained using a weighted combination of the two values. Next, an adaboost detection algorithm is employed and then cascade classiﬁcation is used. Initial classiﬁers are used to remove most negative sam- ples. Next, classiﬁers that achieve low false positive error rates with increased computation are used. This cascade structure can take less time to achieve a high detection rate [6]. The most vulnerable pedestrians are those in the transportation system. Results and discussion Table 1 shows the results for the performance of the proposed at different distances from human to tractor. It can be seen that the performance in morning and evening lighting at 12–20 m provided the highest resolution compared to the other methods. The PDR and FAR at these distance was best; performance was also good at distances of 4–12 m. The accuracy of the proposed algorithm was compared with those of the other algorithms at different distances. The cascade method showed the best accuracy at 0–4 m and showed good results at 4–12 m. At 8–20 m, the proposed algorithm showed good results ( Fig. 10 ). The proposed method was not accurate in comparison with the HOG and cascade methods at 0–4 m when a human is not in the frame in poor light conditions (shade). To produce an over- all algorithm that is highly accurate at all distances under all lighting conditions, combinations using two-by-two and all three algorithms were carried out. Figs. 11–13 show the results of this procedure. Fig. 11 shows that the combination of the proposed algorithm with the cascade algorithm produced the highest accu- racy at 92.2%. Fig. 12 shows that integrating the proposed method with the cascade method provided the best rate of detection of humans at 94.3%. Fig. 13 shows that combining the proposed method with the cascade method produced the lowest FAR at 2.35%. Introduction Machine vision applications vary according to the technique used. Each image contains noise and deformation. Humans do not need to ﬁlter and remove noise to understand what is seen, but machine vision requires this to process an image. One task of vision is to detect and track humans under different environmental conditions. It is difﬁcult to track a human as the object under uncontrolled lighting conditions, in a crowded environment, or when the camera is in motion. These conditions can cause loss of information from the received image, such as the color, texture and shape of the object, which can be important to successful detection of the target. Most methods of target detection use image indices [1–4]. Pedestrian detection is usually done in two steps: feature extrac- tion and classiﬁcation. Feature extraction is preferred over the direct use of the raw pixels from images. One reason is that feature-based systems are quicker than raw pixel-based systems [5]. In the classiﬁcation stage, feature-based systems ﬁrst extract the features and the performance of the classiﬁer is highly depen- dent on the feature extracted. The proper selection of feature extraction and classiﬁcation methods improves the detection rate. Haar-like features are composed of a number of black and white areas for which the intensities of the pixels in the black and white areas are calculated separately. The feature value is obtained using a weighted combination of the two values. Next, an adaboost detection algorithm is employed and then cascade classiﬁcation is used. Initial classiﬁers are used to remove most negative sam- ples. Next, classiﬁers that achieve low false positive error rates with increased computation are used. This cascade structure can take less time to achieve a high detection rate [6]. The most vulnerable pedestrians are those in the transportation system.
